newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Peace in Bosnia depends on factions.
newsitem.headline: Peace in Bosnia depends on factions.

text.p: NATO's top commander said on Tuesday it was up to Bosnia's rival factions to build a lasting peace and international peacekeepers could do no more than provide the conditions.

General George Joulwan told reporters during a visit to Sarajevo that the mandate of the current NATO-led mission, which is due to expire in mid-1998, provided sufficient time for peace to take root in the former Yugoslav republic.

"Two and a half years ought to be enough time to demonstrate whether a nation wants to live in peace," Joulwan said. "We are going to give it that opportunity and in the next 15 months I think there's ample time."
"The idea of reconciliation must take root. If it doesn't, that should be a very clear signal of what lies ahead. But I think we need to put the responsibility where it lies," he said.
The supreme allied commander and Javier Solana, NATO secretary-general, travelled to Sarajevo on Tuesday to hold talks with senior officers in the 31,000-strong Stabilisation Force (SFOR).
SFOR has an 18-month mission to enforce the peace agreement which ended the 1992-95 conflict. A larger multinational force preceded SFOR and served for one year.
Solana and Joulwan met General William Crouch, commander of SFOR in Bosnia, and spoke by telephone to the Croat member of the country's collective presidency, Kresimir Zubak, SFOR spokesmen said.
Solana said that the return of refugees, the reform of Serb and Moslem-Croat federation police forces and adherence to an arms control pact were key elements in preventing a renewal of war.
More than a year after the Dayton peace agreement was signed, few refugees have been allowed to return to areas where rival national groups dominate.
Bosnian police departments, under the firm control of nationalist authorities, have been accused of blocking refugee returns and restricting free movement across ethnic boundary lines.
But Solana said that despite problems with implementing the peace accords, Bosnia had come a long way since fighting ended in November 1995.
Solana recalled staying in the Holiday Inn hotel in wartime near dangerous front lines.

"In this very hotel, a little more than 15 months ago, after being shot at at the airport, I spent a night here without light, without water, without windows and now we're sitting here holding a press conference.
